nodes.name: Sunlight
nodes.desc: Clear shallow water and open slopes let light reach seagrass, algae and the dry-forest canopy.

nodes.name: Warm clear water
nodes.desc: Warm, low-nutrient Caribbean water stays clear, so light reaches the seagrass beds and reefs that ring the island.

nodes.name: Seasonal rain
nodes.desc: Rain on the steep, rocky hillsides drives growth in the dry forest and runs off to the bays.

nodes.name: Thin rocky soil
nodes.desc: Shallow soil on the mountainous island holds the dry forest and is replenished by decomposed leaves.

nodes.name: Bacteria and fungi
nodes.desc: Break down dead seagrass, algae and leaf litter and return nutrients to the sand and soil.

nodes.name: Turtle grass
nodes.desc: Seagrass that covers the sea floor of bays such as Maho Bay and Salt Pond Bay. Green turtles and queen conch graze it.

nodes.name: Reef algae
nodes.desc: A calcified green alga of reefs and sand. Parrotfish, urchins and turtles graze algae like it.

nodes.name: Phytoplankton
nodes.desc: Drifting algae in the open water. They feed zooplankton and, through them, schooling fish.

nodes.name: Dry forest trees
nodes.desc: Gumbo-limbo is a typical tree of the dry to moist forest that covers the island hills. Deer and iguanas browse such foliage.

nodes.name: Zooplankton
nodes.desc: Tiny grazers of phytoplankton that feed sardines and other small fish.

nodes.name: Giant barrel sponge
nodes.desc: A reef sponge that filters tiny particles from the water. Sponges are the main food of hawksbill turtles.

nodes.name: Round sardinella
nodes.desc: A schooling fish that filters plankton and is prey for seabirds and larger fish.

nodes.name: Long-spined sea urchin
nodes.desc: Grazes algae on reefs. A disease killed over 97% of Caribbean Diadema in 1983, and algae then overgrew many reefs.

nodes.name: Stoplight parrotfish
nodes.desc: Scrapes algae from rock and coral, keeping reefs from being overgrown, and excretes the ground rock as sand.

nodes.name: Queen conch
nodes.desc: A large sea snail that grazes algae and seagrass in sandy meadows. It is an important food for turtles and nurse sharks.

nodes.name: Green sea turtle
nodes.desc: Grazes seagrass beds and algae. Sea turtles are seen at Maho Bay.

nodes.name: White-tailed deer
nodes.desc: The most recorded land mammal near the park. It browses leaves and shoots of the dry forest.

nodes.name: Green iguana
nodes.desc: A big leaf-eating lizard of the island forest, preyed on by birds and mammals when young.

nodes.name: Hawksbill sea turtle
nodes.desc: A reef turtle whose diet is mostly sponges, with some algae, mangrove fruit and sea urchins. Mongooses raid its nests in the US Virgin Islands.

nodes.name: Brown pelican
nodes.desc: A plunge-diving fish eater, and one of the park's Important Bird Area species.

nodes.name: Magnificent frigatebird
nodes.desc: The most recorded bird near the park. It snatches fish, squid and jellyfish from the surface and steals food from other seabirds.

nodes.name: Small Indian mongoose
nodes.desc: An introduced predator of lizards, birds and eggs, including sea turtle nests.

nodes.name: Tiger shark
nodes.desc: A top marine predator of the Caribbean that hunts sea turtles among many other prey.
